chapters.title: Chapter 2: Global Cycles That Shaped Modern Markets

lessons.title: From the Roaring Twenties to the Post-War Boom

body.text: The 1929 crash was not what made the Depression last a decade. Policy mistakes that let the credit system collapse did that. The long boom after 1945 happened largely because governments had learned from those mistakes.

children.text: This lesson covers about 45 years, from 1921 to 1966, mostly through the US market, because it was the largest and best documented of its time. It contains the most extreme full cycle in modern market history: an eight-year boom, a fall of almost 90%, a quarter of a century before prices got back to their old peak, and then one of the longest and strongest bull markets ever recorded. The crash of October 1929 is a story of its own. Our focus here is the whole cycle around it, and what it teaches about how deep and how long a downturn can become.
The Roaring Twenties: A Boom With Real Foundations

Like Railway Mania, the 1920s boom started from something real. Electricity reached American homes and factories, cars went into mass production, and radio created a new consumer industry almost overnight. Company profits rose strongly. Two kinds of credit then stretched the boom. Households bought cars, radios and appliances on instalment plans, a new idea at the time. And investors bought shares on margin, often putting down only 10% to 20% of the price and borrowing the rest from their broker. By the late 1920s shoe shiners and office clerks were swapping stock tips, and prices were rising far faster than profits.

children.text: From Crash to Depression: When the Credit Cycle Breaks

By mid November 1929 the Dow had already lost nearly half its value. That was painful, but markets had recovered from falls like it before. What turned a crash into the Great Depression was the next three years. Between 1930 and 1933 thousands of American banks failed, taking depositors' savings with them, and the credit system from Lesson 1.3 went into full reverse. US unemployment reached roughly a quarter of the workforce by 1933. Economists still debate the exact weight of each cause, but most agree that these policy choices made the downturn far deeper and longer than it needed to be.

body.caption: Policy choices that deepened the cycle
headers: What it did to the cycle

cells: The Federal Reserve tightened in 1928 and 1929 to cool stock speculation, and did not flood the system with money once banks began failing
Money supply shrank sharply and bank runs spread from one town to the next
No deposit insurance existed
Any rumour could empty a bank, so even sound banks collapsed
Countries stayed on the gold standard
Central banks could not create money freely without risking their gold, so they kept policy tight in a slump. Countries that left gold earlier, like Britain in 1931, generally recovered sooner
The US raised import duties through the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930
Other countries retaliated, and world trade shrank
Prices were allowed to fall for years
Deflation made every existing loan heavier to repay in real terms, pushing more borrowers into default

body.text: India felt this cycle too. Prices of crops such as wheat, rice and jute collapsed in the early 1930s, crushing farm incomes while land revenue and debts stayed fixed, and adding to rural unrest during the Civil Disobedience Movement. After Britain left the gold standard in 1931, with the rupee tied to sterling, large amounts of so-called distress gold flowed out of India as struggling households sold their jewellery and savings.

body.title: Dow Jones Industrial Average at major turning points, 1921 to 1966

children.text: The points on this chart are turning points, not evenly spaced dates. Two details deserve attention. First, the recovery from 1932 was not a smooth climb. In 1937 the US government cut spending and the Fed tightened bank reserve requirements, believing the recovery was secure. The economy slipped back into recession and the Dow fell by about half in a year, from roughly 194 to 99. Tightening too early can restart a down cycle. Second, it took until November 1954 for the Dow to close above its 1929 peak.

body.label: The longest wait in modern market history
body.value: About 25 years for the Dow to regain its 1929 high
body.context: Peak of 381 in September 1929, first close above it in November 1954. Anyone who bought at the top with borrowed money was wiped out long before then.

body.title: Why the 25-year figure overstates the pain for patient holders

children.text: The index level ignores two things. Companies kept paying dividends, often at high yields once prices had collapsed. And consumer prices fell sharply in the early 1930s, so each dollar bought more. What matters to an investor is the real return, adjusted for inflation or deflation:

content.caption: With deflation, inflation is negative, which lifts the real return above the nominal return

children.text: Example: if your holding is worth exactly what you paid for it, a nominal return of 0%, but prices in the shops have fallen 20%, your real return is 1 ÷ 0.80 − 1 = 25%. Once dividends and deflation are included, several studies estimate that an investor who bought at the 1929 peak and reinvested dividends was back to break-even in real terms in well under half of those 25 years. That is still a brutal wait, but a very different one. The same adjustment works against you in inflationary periods, as Lesson 2.3 shows.

body.title: The Climb Back
body.prompt: The Dow fell from 381 in September 1929 to 41 in July 1932. Using the recovery formula from Lesson 1.1, what percentage gain did it need from the 1932 low to get back to 381? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: Gain needed = 381 ÷ 41 − 1 = 9.29 − 1 = 8.29, or about 829%. The index had to multiply more than nine times just to break even. This is why an 89% fall is in a different category from a 50% fall, which needs a 100% gain.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: An investor's portfolio is worth the same in rupee terms as it was three years ago, but consumer prices have fallen 10% over that period. What is the real return, ignoring dividends?
options: 0%, because the portfolio value has not changed
About +11.1%, because each rupee now buys more
+10%, exactly matching the fall in prices
body.explanation: Real return = (1 + 0) ÷ (1 − 0.10) − 1 = 1 ÷ 0.90 − 1 = 0.111, or about 11.1%. The portfolio buys about 11% more goods than before. It is not exactly 10% because the calculation divides rather than subtracts.

children.text: The Depression produced the modern architecture of financial regulation, and the war produced a new international monetary system. Many of these ideas later travelled to India in some form: deposit insurance, a securities regulator and limits on margin borrowing all exist here today.

body.title: From collapse to a new system, 1933 to 1956

events.title: Banking reform
events.description: The Banking Act of 1933, known as Glass-Steagall, separates commercial banking from investment banking and creates the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, ending the era of routine bank runs. The Securities Act requires companies to disclose information before selling shares to the public. The US also abandons the gold standard for domestic purposes.

events.title: A market regulator
events.description: The Securities Exchange Act creates the Securities and Exchange Commission and gives the Federal Reserve power to set margin requirements, limiting how much investors can borrow to buy shares.

events.title: World War II
events.description: Massive government spending ends mass unemployment in the US. Markets are volatile early in the war and bottom in 1942, before investors begin to anticipate victory.

events.title: Bretton Woods
events.description: Allied nations agree on a system of fixed exchange rates tied to the US dollar, with the dollar convertible into gold. The IMF and the World Bank are created. India is among the founding members.

events.title: The Marshall Plan
events.description: The US funds the rebuilding of Western Europe, reviving trade and demand for American goods.

events.title: The long boom
events.description: Suburbs, highways, cars, television and consumer goods drive strong growth with low inflation. The Dow rises from about 162 in 1949 to about 995 in early 1966.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The US Banking Act of 1933, which separated commercial banking from investment banking, is popularly known as the ___ Act.
body.explanation: Named after its sponsors, Senator Carter Glass and Representative Henry Steagall. Its separation of commercial and investment banking was largely repealed in 1999, which some economists link to the risk-taking that preceded 2008.

children.text: The Post-War Boom: A Long Bull Market With Cycles Inside

markDefs.definition: A long period, often 10 to 20 years or more, during which a market trends upward overall despite shorter bear markets along the way. A secular bear market is the reverse: a long period of flat or falling prices with rallies inside it.

. But look inside it and the shorter cycles never stopped. Investors in that era still lived through several falls of 20% or more, each of which felt at the time like it might be the end of the boom.

body.text: Be careful with the US story: it is the market that survived. Russian shareholders lost everything after the 1917 revolution, the Shanghai stock market closed after 1949, and German investors were devastated by hyperinflation and war. Studying only the market that ended up the world's largest makes long-term equity investing look safer than history says it is. Diversification matters partly because nobody knows in advance which markets will be the survivors.

body.title: Will It Take 25 Years Again?
body.scenario: It is late March 2020. The Nifty has fallen close to 40% in two months. A relative sends a message to the family WhatsApp group: "This is 1929 all over again. After that crash the American market took 25 years to recover. Sell everything and put it in FDs."
body.prompt: Using what you learned in this lesson, what is wrong with this comparison, and what questions would help judge whether a downturn might become long and deep?
body.modelAnswer: The comparison skips why 1929 became a 25-year wait. The crash alone did not do it. Thousands of banks failed with no deposit insurance, the central bank let the money supply shrink, the gold standard stopped policy from responding, tariffs choked trade, and deflation made debts heavier for years. The 25-year figure also ignores dividends and falling prices, which brought patient holders back to break-even in real terms far sooner. In March 2020 the setting was different: the RBI cut rates sharply and injected liquidity, bank deposits in India are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, governments worldwide spent heavily, and the Nifty regained its pre-COVID high within the same year. The useful questions are the ones this lesson raised: Is the banking system holding up? Are central banks easing or tightening? Is credit still flowing? Is there deflation? Those tell you far more about how long a down cycle may last than the size of the first fall. None of this means selling or holding is automatically right, but a decision driven by a misread historical parallel is a poor one.

cards.definition: Buying shares with a small down payment, often 10% to 20%, and borrowing the rest from a broker. It magnified the 1920s boom and the 1929 collapse.
The severe global downturn of the 1930s, deepened by bank failures, tight monetary policy, the gold standard, trade barriers and deflation.
A sustained fall in the general price level. It raises the real burden of debt and can trap an economy in a downward spiral.
Return adjusted for inflation or deflation: (1 + nominal return) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1.
The post-1944 system of fixed exchange rates tied to the US dollar, which was convertible into gold. It created the IMF and the World Bank.
A secular trend lasts a decade or more. Cyclical bull and bear markets are the shorter swings that happen inside it.

body.label: DICGC: Deposit Insurance in India
body.description: The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, a subsidiary of the RBI, insures bank deposits in India. Its site explains current coverage limits and which banks are covered, a direct descendant of the lessons of the 1930s.

children.text: The last row of the bear market table is a warning light. In 1966 the Dow came within a whisker of 1,000, and then went essentially nowhere for 16 years as inflation took hold. Lesson 2.3 covers that long, grinding secular bear market and the great disinflation that ended it.

body.text: Index levels and economic figures in this lesson are approximate and rounded, and historical estimates vary between sources. The content is for education only and is not investment advice. Past market behaviour, in the US or India, does not guarantee future results.

points: The 1920s boom had real foundations in electricity, cars and radio, but instalment credit and margin buying with 10% to 20% down stretched it far beyond earnings
The Dow fell about 89%, from 381 in 1929 to 41 in 1932, needing a gain of about 829% to recover, and did not close above its 1929 peak until November 1954
Bank failures, tight money, the gold standard, tariffs and deflation turned a crash into a decade-long depression, while premature tightening in 1937 caused a second fall of about half
Including dividends and deflation, patient holders recovered in real terms far sooner than 25 years
The 1930s created deposit insurance, securities regulators and margin limits, ideas that exist in India today through DICGC, SEBI and exchange margin rules
The post-war secular bull market took the Dow roughly six times higher from 1949 to 1966, yet still contained four falls of about 19% to 27%
The US is the market that survived. Other markets were wiped out by revolution, war or hyperinflation, which is a strong argument for diversification
